content: Sleep hyperhidrosis, commonly referred to as night sweats, is the occurrence of excessive sweating during sleep. This condition may or may not be accompanied by excessive perspiration during waking hours. Night sweats caused by medical conditions or infections are often described as severe hot flashes that occur at night, capable of soaking sleepwear and bed sheets, and are not related to an overheated environment. When night sweats are suspected to have medical causes, they should be thoroughly investigated by a physician. There are four distinct types of sweating: 1. Diaphoresis: This refers to cold sweats, which are characterized by excessive sweating often associated with medical emergencies such as shock. It is differentiated from hyperhidrosis by the clammy or cold state of the patient. 2. Primary Hyperhidrosis: This condition involves abnormally increased perspiration that exceeds what is necessary for thermoregulation. It is not associated with cold sweats. 3. Secondary Hyperhidrosis: This condition also involves excessive sweating beyond what is required for body temperature regulation but is secondary to an underlying pathological process. Causes may include infections, thyroid or pituitary disorders, diabetes mellitus, tumors, gout, menopause, certain medications, or mercury poisoning. It is not associated with cold sweats. 4. Night Sweats: Sleep hyperhidrosis, or night sweats, involves excessive sweating during sleep. The individual may or may not experience excessive sweating while awake. Sleep hyperhidrosis can occur at any age but is most commonly observed in early adulthood. There are no significant differences in prevalence between men and women. Night sweats may have genetic origins and, in some cases, may be relatively harmless. The natural history of night sweats is unpredictable. Some individuals may experience a self-limited course, while others may suffer from the condition for life. Severe cases can be distressing and disrupt sleep patterns, as the patient may frequently awaken due to the discomfort of damp sleepwear. While some causes, such as menopause, may be relatively benign, night sweats can also indicate serious underlying diseases. One of the most common causes of night sweats in women over 40 is hormonal changes associated with menopause and perimenopause. This is a normal part of menopause and, while bothersome, is not necessarily dangerous or indicative of an underlying disease. Hormonal changes during pregnancy can also lead to night sweats. It is important to distinguish night sweats caused by medical conditions from those resulting from an overly warm sleep environment, such as a hot bedroom or excessive bedding. Night sweats can be caused by a wide range of medical conditions, including but not limited to: Hormonal changes (e.g., menopause, perimenopause, pregnancy) Endocrine disorders (e.g., hyperthyroidism, hypothalamic lesions, diabetes mellitus) Infections (e.g., tuberculosis, endocarditis, pneumonia, malaria, HIV, infectious mononucleosis) Cancers (e.g., lymphoma, leukemia, solid tumors) Medications (e.g., tamoxifen, raloxifene, hydralazine, niacin, tricyclic antidepressants) Neurological conditions (e.g., stroke, post-traumatic syringomyelia) Autoimmune or inflammatory diseases (e.g., sarcoidosis, systemic mastocytosis, temporal arteritis) Substance abuse or withdrawal Obstructive sleep apnea The diagnostic process for night sweats involves a thorough medical history and physical examination. The history should focus on potential infectious and oncologic causes, as well as social factors such as substance abuse and travel history. The physical examination should emphasize the endocrine, dermatologic, and lymphatic systems. Polysomnography (sleep study) may be used to evaluate excessive sweating during sleep, although no specific features have been consistently reported. An echocardiogram may be warranted if there is a high suspicion of endocarditis. Laboratory studies that may aid in identifying the underlying cause include: Complete blood count (CBC) with differential Eosinophil count Urinalysis Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) More advanced tests, such as follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), purified protein derivative (PPD) for tuberculosis, HIV testing with viral load, blood cultures, and thyroid function tests (e.g., free T4), may also be necessary. Imaging studies, such as MRI or CT scans of the chest, abdomen, or pelvis, may be recommended if clinically indicated. Diagnostic criteria for sleep hyperhidrosis include: 1. A complaint of excessive sweating during sleep. 2. Polysomnography with quinizarin powder applied to affected areas, demonstrating excessive sweating during sleep. 3. Exclusion of other medical disorders, such as febrile illnesses or diabetes insipidus, as the primary cause. 4. Recognition that other conditions, such as obstructive sleep apnea, may coexist and contribute to the disorder. Severity of night sweats can be classified as follows: Mild: No bathing or clothing change required; the patient may need to turn the pillow or remove blankets. Moderate: Sleep is disturbed by the need to wash the face or other affected areas, but no clothing change is necessary. Severe: Bathing or a change of clothing is required. Duration criteria are categorized as: Acute: Symptoms lasting one month or less. Subacute: Symptoms lasting more than one month but less than six months. Chronic: Symptoms persisting for six months or longer.
